national.title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
national.summary: Trump welcomes the outcome, praising Hegseth as a "Great American Patriot", but Democrats can try again next year.
national.body:
An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.

A majority of the House of Representatives voted to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, for now.

In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".

The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.

However, that calculation could change in January when the Democratic Party assumes control of both chambers of Congress, following its successes in the US midterm elections. For now, Trump's Republican Party remains in control.

After Tuesday's vote, the most senior Democrat in the House, Hakeem Jeffries, said: "This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning."

The question on which lawmakers were voting on Tuesday was whether or not to refer the resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, which is led by Republicans. The alternative would have been to allow the resolution to proceed in the House itself.

All Republicans other than Massie voted to refer the resolution to the committee, meaning that the congressman's effort failed in a 211-204 vote.

national.title: Nima Momeni gets 16 years to life for murder of Cash App founder Bob Lee
national.summary: Nima Momeni, the man convicted in the 2023 killing of Cash App founder Bob Lee in San Francisco​, was sentenced to 16 years to life in prison on Tuesday.
national.body: Nima Momeni, the man convicted in the 2023 killing of Cash App founder Bob Lee in San Francisco, was sentenced to 16 years to life in prison on Tuesday.Momeni was convicted of second-degree murder in December 2024 for fatally stabbing Lee in the city's East Cut neighborhood under the Bay Bridge in April 2023, a killing that fueled a "doom loop" narrative about San Francisco street crime following the COVID pandemic. Prosecutors said Momeni stabbed Lee following an argument about Momeni's sister and her relationship with Lee, along with their ongoing drug use. Momeni was found not guilty of premeditated first-degree murder. During the trial, his lawyers claimed he acted in self-defense, alleging that Lee had lunged at Momeni with a knife while under the influence of drugs and that Lee became aggressive after Momeni made a "bad joke" at the expense of Lee's family.Aside from creating the Cash App digital wallet, Lee was a former chief technology officer for e-commerce company Square, Inc. and was chief product officer of the cryptocurrency MobileCoin at the time of his death.His killing amplified a narrative of San Francisco spiraling into lawlessness, with high-profile figures such as Elon Musk driving the perception on social media. City officials aggressively pushed back against the sensationalist nature of the narrative, especially after it was quickly determined the stabbing was not a random street crime but rather stemmed from a personal dispute.The sentencing was delayed extensively following a series of post-trial maneuvers from Momeni's defense team that included motions for a new trial and a new group of defense attorneys. The judge ultimately dismissed the challenges and requests for a retrial.

national.title: U.S. soldier accused of spying linked to Russia arrested in the U.K.
national.summary: A U.S. official told CBS News the suspect is a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters for NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
national.body: A U.S. Army soldier has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia, British and U.S. authorities announced Tuesday.The 41-year-old suspect was not identified, but a U.S. official told CBS News he is a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. He was arrested Tuesday near Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London.The soldier is suspected of violations under Section 1 and Section 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 — obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service, respectively. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia and that the force was carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire — the county where the base is located — related to the investigation.The suspect was in custody in a London police station as of Tuesday, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command. "The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing force, said in a statement. "This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved. We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security." FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that "this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."Speaking to reporters Wednesday in Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had "nothing to do with" the detention of the U.S. soldier.In an annual threat update last month, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of Britain's MI5 spy agency, accused Russia of "escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," calling them "aggressor number one" when it comes to threats against the United Kingdom.The arrest came as the U.S., Russia and Ukraine began a new round of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, the first such talks aimed at ending the war between Russia and Ukraine in about nine months. national.title: 4 grizzly bears killed mom and daughter in Canada, DNA confirms
national.summary: DNA tests linked four bears to the deaths of Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed, officials said. All four bears were killed to protect the public.
national.body: Four grizzly bears captured in western Canada were responsible for killing a mother and her adult daughter this month in what investigators believe was a rare predatory attack, wildlife officials said Tuesday. DNA tests conclusively linked a female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the deaths of Jenny Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said. All four bears were killed to protect the public. "Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare," Inspector Jeff Tyre told an online briefing. "That is to say, we don't know how it started, but we know how it ended." The women's remains were found about 150 meters (490 feet) apart near a trail outside Bella Coola, a remote community about 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) north of Vancouver. Family members raised the alarm after Reed missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister. Searchers found her mother's remains first, then discovered Reed's remains in a bear cache, where bears store food. Tyre said the bears were not involved in a separate grizzly attack last November on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area. Eleven people were injured, including two critically.The latest killings have shaken the Nuxalk Nation community, which is still recovering from last year's attack. Local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew, and police escorted children to school. "This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack," said Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, the Nuxalk Nation's elected chief councilor. He said community support services would remain available as long as needed. Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks cannot be rehabilitated or relocated because they pose an extreme risk to public safety."This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," Tyre said. national.title: Eswatini gives illegal foreign businesses 12 months to leave
national.summary: The law follows the growth of foreign-owned businesses in retail sector in rural areas.
national.body:
Businesses owned by Asian nationals are being closed across Eswatini as the government cracks down on foreign-owned enterprises.

The crackdown follows Parliament's approval of the Citizen Economic Empowerment Act, which seeks to increase ownership and participation by emaSwati, as citizens in the kingdom are known.

The legislation follows complaints from local traders that foreign-owned businesses are encroaching on traditional retail markets, increasing competition and threatening livelihoods.

South Africa has witnessed more severe enforcement actions, including raids, arrests and the disruption of foreign-run informal businesses, while Kenya has also stepped up action against foreign traders.

Its implementation has sparked a heated debate in Parliament, with MPs divided over how quickly foreign businesses owners should be required to leave.

Mbabane East MP Welcome Dlamini told Parliament on Tuesday that officials from the trade ministry had already begun enforcing the law by closing Asian-owned shops.

Hhohho Regional MP Tanele Magagula called for immediate action, saying "Businesses owned by foreigners in the rural areas must be seized immediately."

But Dlamini questioned whether local entrepreneurs were ready to take over the businesses, arguing that foreigner should be given time tio train their successors.

national.summary: A U.S. federal judge has denied a motion to dismiss President Trump's defamation case against the BBC, allowing the case to proceed.
national.body: A U.S. federal judge denied a motion on Tuesday to dismiss President Trump's defamation case against the BBC, allowing the case to proceed.In December 2025, Mr. Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation, the U.K.'s public broadcaster, over a documentary that featured edited parts of the speech he delivered on Jan. 6, 2021, as his supporters massed around the U.S. Capitol in what would become an assault on the heart of the government.In the lawsuit, filed in the Southern District of Florida, attorneys for Mr. Trump accuse the BBC of publishing a "false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory and malicious depiction" of him in an episode of the network's "Panorama" program, which aired a week before the 2024 election.The case alleges the BBC "intentionally and maliciously sought to fully mislead its viewers" by "splicing together" two clips of the same speech Mr. Trump gave to supporters before the riots began. The president's legal team claims the two clips were 55 minutes apart and the edit omitted "his statement calling for peace."On Tuesday, Judge Jeffrey Kuntz denied the BBC's motion to dismiss the defamation case, effectively allowing it to proceed."Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," Kuntz wrote in his decision.Mr. Trump hailed the decision as "A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth," in a post on his Truth Social platform.A spokesperson for the BBC, quoted by the network's news division, said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage.""We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process," the spokesperson added.On Oct. 22, a federal judge in Miami said Mr. Trump must sit for a deposition with BBC lawyers by Dec. 11, warning that if he did not, he could face penalties, including possible dismissal of the lawsuit, unless the period for the president and the network to collect information in the case is extended.Mr. Trump had been due to sit for a deposition in October, but his lawyers told the BBC in late September that he would no longer be available to answer questions, "due to other matters of national importance."The president has said he will be avai

national.title: Trump's judicial confirmations to face resistance in Democratic-controlled Senate
national.summary: A Democratic-controlled Senate is unlikely to help President Trump and Republicans continue their push to remake the federal judiciary in the next two years.
national.body: Washington — After seeing success in reshaping the federal judiciary in his first term and the initial two years of his second administration, President Trump and Republicans' campaign to shift the courts to the right could be coming to an end with Democrats poised to take control of the Senate next year.During his first term in office, Mr. Trump successfully put more than 230 judges on the federal bench, including three justices on the Supreme Court, remaking the judicial branch for decades. So far during his second term, the Senate has confirmed 57 of the president's judicial picks. In total, Trump nominees make up about one-third of active federal judges.But Democrats are now poised to control at least 54 Senate seats, and as many as 56 depending on the outcome of races in Mississippi and Alaska, making it unlikely that Mr. Trump will fill many more vacancies on the U.S. district and appeals courts."No one, or nearly no one, is going to get confirmed, so what he does in terms of nominating people, we'll see," Ed Whelan, a distinguished senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center and former law clerk to the late Justice Antonin Scalia, told CBS News.There are currently 28 vacancies on the federal courts and another 15 seats that will open up in the coming weeks and months. So far, the president has formally sent to the Senate 16 nominees for those existing and future vacancies, though it's possible he submits more names for consideration before the current Congress finishes its work. Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social earlier Tuesday three more nominees to district courts in Texas and South Carolina.The GOP-led Senate Judiciary Committee is moving quickly to advance those picks before control of the upper chamber changes hands. It voted to advance four of the president's district court candidates and held confirmation hearings for four other judicial nominees Tuesday.The panel is expected to hold more confirmation hearings next week, a break from committee practice of holding those proceedings every other week, according to a source familiar with the panel's workings.Republicans are violating "numerous longstanding standards in a desperate attempt to confirm more than 30 qualified loyalists to lifetime appointments before Democrats take the majority," Sen. national.summary: Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV, HAS DIED. hE WAS 85.
national.body: Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85. Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, "after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure," his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017. Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favorite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating "World's Most Amazing Videos" on TV. He played a deranged colonel in "The Ninth Configuration" (also known as "Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane"), led the TV show "Titus," had a role in Alexander Payne's Oscar-nominated drama "Nebraska," and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama "Blue Bloods." Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney's bitter father in "Jay Kelly." "My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career," he told New York magazine in 2012. "My choices have had a cost attached to it. But I've gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III, and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything.""One of the greats" Actor Lou Diamond Phillips, who played Keach's son in the 2008 TV movie "Lone Rider," said in a post on X that Keach was a "consummate actor, gracious, giving and incredibly kind even while he had the presence of a smoldering volcano. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him." national.title: Both sides now? Critics slam DOJ moves to dismiss convictions of Trump allies
national.summary: The DOJ moved to dismiss criminal convictions of former Trump adviser Steve Bannon and of the Oath Keepers, in what it calls "the interests of justice." Critics are crying foul.
national.body:
The Biden-era Justice Department portrayed the contempt of Congress case against Steve Bannon as open and shut.

Bannon declined to cooperate with the House committee that investigated the siege on the U.S. Capitol, flouting a subpoena and refusing to show up for an interview. A trial jury in Washington, D.C., deliberated for less than three hours before delivering a guilty verdict . A federal appeals court upheld that verdict.

Now, four years later, the DOJ is asking a court to drop the case and erase the conviction "in the interests of justice." Bannon's lawyers do not oppose the move.

Legal experts said it follows a pattern where the Justice Department is helping to wipe the slate clean for allies of President Trump—with no one defending the cases, and without courts hearing arguments to the contrary. That violates the U.S. legal system's tradition of hearing views from opposing parties and comes as the Justice Department has also pursued investigations of Trump's perceived enemies .

"No adversity remains in this serious and high-profile criminal matter between, on the one hand, the U.S. Department of Justice overtly acting at the behest of the president of the United States, and on the other hand, Bannon, the defendant, who is a close political ally and adviser to the same president," said Bruce Searby, a defense attorney in Washington and a former federal prosecutor.

The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment about its decision to walk away from the conviction and the lack of adversity, or truly opposing parties, in the case. Bannon's lawyers did not return messages seeking comment.

Law Judge accuses DOJ of 'weaponization,' tosses case against ex-FBI officials Vacating convictions, issuing pardons Searby first noticed the issue in April, when the DOJ asked to vacate the convictions of about a dozen leaders and deputies of the far-right Oath Keepers and Proud Boys groups.

Those seditious conspiracy trials took months to unfold, as juries heard details about how some of those extremists gathered weapons, recruited followers and even breached the Capitol in the worst attack since the War of 1812.

national.title: Volunteer musicians play songs for veterans who are hospitalized
national.summary: Volunteer musicians play for veterans and others who are hospitalized. They're part of Musicians On Call, a group that spreads the healing power of music.
national.body:
After playing and singing "Little Wonders," by Rob Thomas for Army veteran John Fay at the DC VA Medical Center's Hospice Unit, Musicians On Call performer, Dante Ciolfi, thanks Fay for his service. Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR hide caption

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Dante Ciolfi unzips his guitar case in a courtyard of the Veterans Medical Center in Washington, D.C.

He is getting ready to play some songs for patients in the hospice wing of the hospital. Ciolfi is a musician volunteer with Musicians On Call or MOC, a non-profit that brings live music to hospital patients nationwide, both bedside and virtually via zoom. The group's motto is "delivering the healing power of music." When Ciolfi isn't volunteering, he teaches computer science to graduate students.

He meets up with Ellen Morris, another volunteer with MOC. She trains musician volunteers on hospital protocols and guides them from room to room.

Once they reach the hospital's hospice unit, Morris takes the lead and knocks on a patient's room door. "Hi there, how are you doing today? My name is Ellen with Musicians on Call," she says, "I have my friend Dante here that would love to play a song for you today, would that be OK?"

The patient, 93-year old Army veteran Lawrence Ludden, agrees. He is sitting in his room reading the newspaper, but he's quick to extend his hand to visitors.

Ciolfi thanks Ludden for the sacrifices he's made then he adjusts his guitar and begins singing, "Desperado," by the Eagles.

Ludden's room is filled with sunlight. His daughter Eillen Ludden is here on her daily visit.

national.title: Oil giant ExxonMobil left Venezuela years ago. Now it's considering a return
national.summary: ExxonMobil has signed a memorandum of understanding with the Venezuelan government and its state-owned oil company to explore opportunities in the country.
national.body:
ExxonMobil, the biggest U.S. oil company, is exploring a return to Venezuela after leaving almost two decades ago.

On Monday, the company announced it had signed a memorandum of understanding with the Venezuelan government and its state-owned oil company, Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. The MOU, which is typically a non-binding agreement, involves ExxonMobil examining potential "upstream opportunities" – that refers to oil exploration and production.

ExxonMobil said in a statement, "We welcome the opportunity to evaluate potential upstream opportunities with the Venezuelan government and PDVSA."

A lot has happened in Venezuela's oil sector in the past ten months. In January, shortly after the Trump administration captured Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, Trump gathered U.S. oil company executives in the White House and urged them to invest in the country. At that time, ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods said the country was "uninvestable."

But the country overhauled its petroleum law this year to make it more attractive for international oil companies. Those changes included allowing private oil companies more operational control in partnerships, as well as reforming taxes and royalties. The country has also welcomed the expansion of other U.S. oil companies, including Chevron and Continental Resources.

Still, ExxonMobil executives have maintained a cautious tone. On a call with analysts last month, Woods said that while there is "progress being made on those areas– working on fiscal regimes, working on legal regimes, working on investor protections, a number of things that are kind of in progress. But there's a way to go."

"This memorandum is a meaningful first step," ExxonMobil's statement reads, "But any future investment would require stable policies, clear regulations, strong investment protections and competitive returns."

ExxonMobil, which grew out of Standard Oil, operated in Venezuela for much of the 20th century. But over the years, the company's relationship with the Venezuelan government has been rocky. Beginning in 2004, then-President Hugo Chávez forcibly renegotiated contracts with international oil companies and ordered the nationalization of ExxonMobil assets. In 2007, ExxonMobil left the country.

national.title: U.S. officials look to Europe to learn how to make prison better
national.summary: American prison officials are looking to European nations like Germany and Norway for a roadmap on how to design a prison that emphasizes rehabilitation and a successful return to life on the outside.
national.body:
A group of Americans, whose work intersects with the criminal justice system in New York City, tour the Moabit pretrial detention facility in Berlin, Germany. The nonprofit Vera Institute of Justice invites officials to tour prisons in Germany to see how they design their system for rehabilitation. Lena Mucha hide caption

More than a dozen New Yorkers crowded into an empty prison cell in Berlin, Germany, this October. Inside, they found many contrasts to U.S. prisons: For one, prisoners held at this German facility, Tegel Prison, have keys to their own cells.

The reason, prison director Martin Riemer told the group, is so the men held here can lock their own door when they go to work or school, just like someone might at home. The guards still have keys, but Riemer said this gesture offers a semblance of privacy.

Riemer also noted that every prison cell in Germany must have natural light and ventilation. In the cell the tour group inspected, the large window still had bars on it, but it opened. A breeze was blowing in.

The purpose of this trip was to inspire key players in the criminal justice system — a judge, a prosecutor, a prison official, among others — to see new ways of improving New York City's troubled jail system , which officials are in the process of reimagining.

The trip, organized by the Vera Institute of Justice, a criminal justice reform nonprofit, is part of a larger trend: U.S. officials are increasingly looking abroad for how to design a better prison or jail system. In fact, at least 10 U.S. states now model some of their prison units or practices after prison systems in Western Europe and Scandinavia.

"It's what happens when they get there that makes a world of difference, really seeing it with their own eyes," says Nancy La Vigne, dean of the Rutgers School of Criminal Justice. "Touring the facilities, talking to the officers, talking to the incarcerated population, witnessing rehabilitation in real time is very inspiring."

Every time I host Thanksgiving, it feels like a debate between what to repeat from last year and what to do differently this year.

Should I cook that turkey recipe again, or try a new one? Should I decorate the table with mini gourds again, or shake things up with a big sunflower centerpiece?

Let Life Kit help you decide. As you plan your Thanksgiving, friendsgiving or harvest-themed dinner party menu and decor, here are a few fresh ideas to add flavor, color and calm to the day. That includes two foolproof turkey recipes, advice on how to stay present while hosting, and directions on how to create a stunning floral arrangement with supermarket flowers.

Combine these recipes with sides and desserts — and you've got a whole feast. Don't forget to make Mama Stamberg's cranberry relish !

national.title: AI hoaxes are deceiving 911 dispatchers, and they're only getting harder to detect
national.summary: Swatters are increasingly using AI technology that creates synthetic voices or sound effects to generate remarkably believable fake emergency calls to law enforcement.
national.body:
In August, a caller made a bomb threat to Wheatland Union High School in Yuba County, Calif.

Police responded overnight and classes were canceled. There was no bomb and no one was hurt.

The Indicator from Planet Money Fighting AI with AI Authorities said it was part of a series of hoax calls — also called swatting — made to schools across the country over the summer.

Swatting calls can be made to 911 or police departments, with callers reporting a bomb threat, mass shooting or some other kind of life-threatening emergency with the intention of initiating a massive emergency response, according to the FBI .

911 dispatchers have long dealt with this problem. But the incident in Yuba County was different: The call was made by an AI-generated voice, a new and growing challenge for emergency responders.

"Those voices [of swatting callers] used to be pretty easy to recognize, but now they're natural sounding. They can insert pauses. They can use words like, 'uh', or 'maybe, um, let me think about it.' And it sounds very natural," says Mel Maier, the CEO and executive director of APCO International, the Association of Public Safety Communication Officials.

The goal of swatting calls is to harass or retaliate against the targets of the calls — like a public official. They usually trigger a big, chaotic response from police, redirecting public safety resources from real emergencies.

People also have been killed and injured in swatting attacks, Maier notes.

national.title: Oil giant ExxonMobil left Venezuela years ago. Now it's considering a return
national.summary: ExxonMobil has signed a memorandum of understanding with the Venezuelan government and its state-owned oil company to explore opportunities in the country.
national.body:
ExxonMobil, the biggest U.S. oil company, is exploring a return to Venezuela after leaving almost two decades ago.

On Monday, the company announced it had signed a memorandum of understanding with the Venezuelan government and its state-owned oil company, Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. The MOU, which is typically a non-binding agreement, involves ExxonMobil examining potential "upstream opportunities" – that refers to oil exploration and production.

ExxonMobil said in a statement, "We welcome the opportunity to evaluate potential upstream opportunities with the Venezuelan government and PDVSA."

A lot has happened in Venezuela's oil sector in the past ten months. In January, shortly after the Trump administration captured Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, Trump gathered U.S. oil company executives in the White House and urged them to invest in the country. At that time, ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods said the country was "uninvestable."

But the country overhauled its petroleum law this year to make it more attractive for international oil companies. Those changes included allowing private oil companies more operational control in partnerships, as well as reforming taxes and royalties. The country has also welcomed the expansion of other U.S. oil companies, including Chevron and Continental Resources.

Still, ExxonMobil executives have maintained a cautious tone. On a call with analysts last month, Woods said that while there is "progress being made on those areas– working on fiscal regimes, working on legal regimes, working on investor protections, a number of things that are kind of in progress. But there's a way to go."

"This memorandum is a meaningful first step," ExxonMobil's statement reads, "But any future investment would require stable policies, clear regulations, strong investment protections and competitive returns."

ExxonMobil, which grew out of Standard Oil, operated in Venezuela for much of the 20th century. But over the years, the company's relationship with the Venezuelan government has been rocky. Beginning in 2004, then-President Hugo Chávez forcibly renegotiated contracts with international oil companies and ordered the nationalization of ExxonMobil assets. In 2007, ExxonMobil left the country.

national.title: Volunteer musicians play songs for veterans who are hospitalized
national.summary: Volunteer musicians play for veterans and others who are hospitalized. They're part of Musicians On Call, a group that spreads the healing power of music.
national.body:
After playing and singing "Little Wonders," by Rob Thomas for Army veteran John Fay at the DC VA Medical Center's Hospice Unit, Musicians On Call performer, Dante Ciolfi, thanks Fay for his service. Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR hide caption

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Dante Ciolfi unzips his guitar case in a courtyard of the Veterans Medical Center in Washington, D.C.

He is getting ready to play some songs for patients in the hospice wing of the hospital. Ciolfi is a musician volunteer with Musicians On Call or MOC, a non-profit that brings live music to hospital patients nationwide, both bedside and virtually via zoom. The group's motto is "delivering the healing power of music." When Ciolfi isn't volunteering, he teaches computer science to graduate students.

He meets up with Ellen Morris, another volunteer with MOC. She trains musician volunteers on hospital protocols and guides them from room to room.

Once they reach the hospital's hospice unit, Morris takes the lead and knocks on a patient's room door. "Hi there, how are you doing today? My name is Ellen with Musicians on Call," she says, "I have my friend Dante here that would love to play a song for you today, would that be OK?"

The patient, 93-year old Army veteran Lawrence Ludden, agrees. He is sitting in his room reading the newspaper, but he's quick to extend his hand to visitors.

Ciolfi thanks Ludden for the sacrifices he's made then he adjusts his guitar and begins singing, "Desperado," by the Eagles.

Ludden's room is filled with sunlight. His daughter Eillen Ludden is here on her daily visit.

national.title: U.S. officials look to Europe to learn how to make prison better
national.summary: American prison officials are looking to European nations like Germany and Norway for a roadmap on how to design a prison that emphasizes rehabilitation and a successful return to life on the outside.
national.body:
A group of Americans, whose work intersects with the criminal justice system in New York City, tour the Moabit pretrial detention facility in Berlin, Germany. The nonprofit Vera Institute of Justice invites officials to tour prisons in Germany to see how they design their system for rehabilitation. Lena Mucha hide caption

More than a dozen New Yorkers crowded into an empty prison cell in Berlin, Germany, this October. Inside, they found many contrasts to U.S. prisons: For one, prisoners held at this German facility, Tegel Prison, have keys to their own cells.

The reason, prison director Martin Riemer told the group, is so the men held here can lock their own door when they go to work or school, just like someone might at home. The guards still have keys, but Riemer said this gesture offers a semblance of privacy.

Riemer also noted that every prison cell in Germany must have natural light and ventilation. In the cell the tour group inspected, the large window still had bars on it, but it opened. A breeze was blowing in.

The purpose of this trip was to inspire key players in the criminal justice system — a judge, a prosecutor, a prison official, among others — to see new ways of improving New York City's troubled jail system , which officials are in the process of reimagining.

The trip, organized by the Vera Institute of Justice, a criminal justice reform nonprofit, is part of a larger trend: U.S. officials are increasingly looking abroad for how to design a better prison or jail system. In fact, at least 10 U.S. states now model some of their prison units or practices after prison systems in Western Europe and Scandinavia.

"It's what happens when they get there that makes a world of difference, really seeing it with their own eyes," says Nancy La Vigne, dean of the Rutgers School of Criminal Justice. "Touring the facilities, talking to the officers, talking to the incarcerated population, witnessing rehabilitation in real time is very inspiring."

Aisha Elliott (in red jacket) and Tina Luongo, both seated, listen during a tour of a suicide prevention room at the Moabit pretrial detention facility in Berlin. Lena Mucha hide caption

national.title: Spain's first general strike in 14 years demands solutions to housing crisis
national.summary: Less than three weeks before a national election that could catapult the far right to power, Spain's workers are striking on Wednesday to demand that the government remedy the nation's housing crisis.
national.body:
A woman walks through Atocha train station during a nationwide general strike over the country's housing crisis in Madrid, Spain, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Francisco Seco/AP hide caption

BARCELONA, Spain — Less than three weeks before a national election that could catapult the far right to power, millions of Spain's workers are striking on Wednesday to demand that the government remedy the nation's housing crisis.

The general strike — Spain's first in 14 years — is causing delays in the public transport system and slowing down factories across the eurozone's fourth-largest economy. Many schools and universities reportedly closed or are working at minimal capacity. In the capital, Madrid, this adds to an ongoing strike started by teachers nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions.

In Barcelona, the country's second-largest city, public transport was at a standstill or facing long delays in the morning rush hour. In Madrid, which saw heavy rains in the morning, city buses were the hardest affected. Unions have called for Madrid workers to gather and march through the city center later Wednesday. Marches and gatherings are also planned in Barcelona and other cities.

The two main unions calling for the strike, UGT and CCOO, said in a statement that there was widespread participation, "with significant work stoppages in strategic sectors" — 90% in the automotive and port sectors, 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection, and 75% in the energy sector.

"It's extremely important to remind people that we, the workers — who are also renters or who also pay mortgages — are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill," Sandra Mora, spokesperson for the Tenants' Union, told the national radio, RNE.

Minor incidents were reported in the first hours of the strike, including roadblocks — some with burning tires — in Barcelona, and scuffles between picketers and police near the country's main wholesale market on Madrid's outskirts.

Earlier, at the stroke of midnight on Wednesday, striking workers set off fireworks as they gathered in public squares in Barcelona.

national.title: Grim details emerge after bears kill woman and daughter
national.summary: The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain and the grizzly bears' behavior.
national.body: Selah Reed's family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister. When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia's central coast. Balcarras' car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found. Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras' brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly. When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found. The search was now a tragic recovery effort.The killings of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 1.8 to 2.4 miles from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack. Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend's attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. On Nov. 11, the conservation service said forensic testing had confirmed that four bears — an adult female and her three offspring — captured in the traps were involved in the attack that killed Balcarras and her daughter."After considering the evidence and in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines, conservation officers dispatched all four bears to protect public safety," the agency said, adding that the investigation "found that the encounter likely involved predatory behavior.""This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," Tyre said in the new statement.The forensic testing also confirmed that the bears involved in the recent attack were not the same animals behind the attack on the school children

national.title: Tearful Smith switches allegiance to Netherlands
national.summary: Tatjana Smith, South Africa's most decorated Olympian, switches allegiance to the Netherlands.
national.body:
South Africa's most decorated Olympian Tatjana Smith was in tears as she announced that she has switched allegiance to the Netherlands.

The 29-year-old won four Olympic breaststroke medals, including two golds, before retiring after the Paris 2024 Games.

She came out of retirement in September and hopes to compete in the 50m breaststroke as the event makes its Olympic debut at the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.

Smith, whose maiden name was Schoenmaker, wiped away tears as she read a letter addressed to South Africa, saying that "dreams can change as we grow".

She said she has "always been Dutch and South African" and that this is an opportunity to "explore another part of my identity and heritage that I've never experienced through sport".

She said it also offers her "greater high-performance support and the potential to build a more sustainable career" because the "financial and practical challenges of swimming were among the reasons my previous career became difficult to sustain".

Smith has previously said that financial worries, which included a dispute with Swimming South Africa over prize money, contributed to her decision to step away from the sport.

Smith won four world and Commonwealth gold medals between 2018 and 2023.

national.title: Rubio says U.S. has "no need" to restart combat operations in Iran
national.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he saw no need to resume major combat operations against Iran because economic sanctions were working so effectively.
national.body:
The Justice Department on Tuesday announced charges against three men described as "Iranian operatives" over their alleged role in an alleged terrorist plot at Britain's RAF Fairford airbase .

Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani were charged in relation to the September incident at the base, which has been used by the U.S. military in its operations against Iran.

"To date, the subjects have been allegedly involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States in support of Kata'ib Hizballah and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.

Al-Saadi, 32, is a citizen of Iraq and Iran; Mohajeri, 48, is a citizen of Iran; and Al-Hassani, 35, is a citizen of Iraq, according to the DOJ.

They are charged with conspiring to provide material support to a foreign terrorist organization, conspiring to provide material support for acts of terrorism, providing material support for acts of terrorism, conspiring to bomb a place of public use and financing terrorism.

Separately, Al-Saadi is charged with attempted acts of terrorism transcending national boundaries and attempted destruction of property by means of fire or explosive.

Hours after the Iranian foreign ministry officially rejected any responsibility for grocery store refrigerators being hacked across the country, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi added insult to injury.

"Unable to manage fridges let alone addressing grievances of its people, French government is shifting blame for its failures onto others," Araghchi wrote on X .

national.title: Bessent relocates from home to base after Iran threats, reports say
national.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C. area to a military base following an Iranian threat against his life, reports say.
national.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C. area to a military base following an Iranian threat against his life, The New York Times reported, followed by the Reuters news agency. Both cited people familiar with the matter.CBS News has reached out to the Treasury Department and White House for comment.Bessent has spearheaded a U.S. push to cripple Iran's economy, vowing an "economic onslaught" against Tehran through a web of sanctions.U.S. national intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned last month that Iran has "substantially increased" its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond.Those efforts include beefing up the targeting of current and former U.S. officials such as Bessent, the Times reported. Iranian plotting against U.S. officials has reached a "more advanced stage," according to the anonymous sources, but the severity of the threats against Bessent was unclear. A Treasury Department spokesperson said in a statement to the Times that Bessent "will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats" and that he is still committed to his campaign to squeeze Iran's economy. Clayton's warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, came as the State Department adjusted staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pared back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen. The U.S. military has also removed some aircraft from two British bases in recent weeks following reported threats from Iran. Diplomatic efforts to end the war are gathering steam, with Rubio saying on Tuesday that he saw no need to resume major combat operations against Iran because economic sanctions and other restrictions were working so effectively.

national.title: Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak
national.summary: Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease.
national.body:
A healthcare worker walks by a young patient inside an Ebola treatment center in Beni, North Kivu Province, Congo, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP hide caption

BUNIA, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease.

Global Health The Ebola outbreak is breaking records — and just marked a grim milestone According to the latest health ministry data, 11,042 people have been infected with the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387 — nearly half of those infected in what has been Congo's deadliest outbreak.

The outbreak was declared in mid-May, and since then, Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to several factors, including armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.

The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces.

The resurgence of violence in the two major hotspots in Ituri and North Kivu provinces has sparked worry among health authorities who are calling for a halt to the fighting to allow health workers unhindered access to the sick.

Health facilities and medical professionals have also been targeted by many in communities skeptical of the virus, and there have been several attacks on health workers.

Experts have called for more efforts to slow and contain the disease in Congo, while it has spread to multiple African countries including Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

national.title: What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
national.summary: The billionaire tech executive finds himself mired in a personal and national security scandal.
national.body:
One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report.

Jensen Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the affair.

It said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Jensen Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company.

US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.

However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

national.title: US warns Madagascar over growing military ties with Russia
national.summary: US general warns the Sahel model-like security deal with Russia could lead to greater instability in Africa.
national.body:
The US has warned Madagascar against strengthening its ties with Russia, saying similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security.

US Africa Command deputy head Lt Gen John Brennan said Madagascar's strategic location in the Indian Ocean made it important to global trade.

He warned against what he called the "Sahel model", which he said risked fuelling instability across the continent.

Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, all under military rule, have reduced ties with the Western partners and turned to Russia to support their fight against jihadist groups.

Russia has expanded its co-operation with Madagascar since the army seized power in 2025, supplying weapons and military instructors.

"We are concerned about Russia wanting to proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent," Brennan told reporters in an online briefing.

"Madagascar sits in a location that is extremely important, as is Mozambique, and we don't want to see those models be applied in those two locations," he said.

The three Sahel countries had blamed their former Western partners for failing to contain jihadist violence before turning to Moscow.

national.title: GOP picks leaders, blocks Hegseth impeachment
national.summary: House and Senate Republicans held internal elections for their leadership teams on Tuesday as they prepare to become the minority in January.
national.body:
Seven Republicans and 11 Democrats missed Tuesday's vote to effectively block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The vote passed 211-204, with 203 Democrats and GOP Rep. Thomas Massie voting no.

The Democrats who did not vote were Reps. Julia Brownley, Lou Correa, Laura Gillen, Steven Horsford, Jonathan Jackson, Nancy Pelosi, Brittany Pettersen, Melanie Stansbury, Haley Stevens, Marilyn Strickland and Frederica Wilson.

The non-voting Republicans were Reps. Monica De La Cruz, Neal Dunn, Russell Fry, Julia Letlow, Tom Tiffany, Derrick Van Orden and Rudy Yakym.

Stansbury, a New Mexico Democrat, said in a statement on social media that she was "blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote."

"When she reached the chamber, the vote had just gaveled out. She immediately filed a report of her vote of 'NO' to the motion meant to kill the impeachment articles and refer them to the Judiciary Committee, as documented in the Congressional Record," the statement read. "Pete Hegseth must be impeached now."

Correa, a California Democrat, said earlier Tuesday he is remaining in his district due to a medical procedure.

Nearly a dozen Democrats skipped Tuesday night's vote on the impeachment resolution, helping Republicans defeat it through a motion to refer it to the Judiciary Committee. The move effectively kills the resolution.

national.title: At least 3 killed when SUV crashes into North Hollywood food stand
national.summary: At least three people were killed and three others injured when an SUV crashed into a food stand near a Metro bus stop in North Hollywood.
national.body: At least three people are dead after an SUV crashed into a food stand near a North Hollywood bus stop in Los Angeles on Tuesday night. The collision occurred at around 5:55 p.m. local time near the Metro station at the corner of Lankershim and Chandler boulevards, according to the LA Fire Department. Firefighters said three people were pronounced dead at the scene, while three others were taken to a nearby hospital, two of whom were in critical condition at the time. As of 11 p.m., one of the victims remained in stable condition, while the other was still critical.Crews extricated one person from the wreckage, according to LAFD."I'm heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted," Mayor Karen Bass wrote in a statement on X. "We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."LA Police Department officers said the driver of the white SUV, a man in his 60s, was one of the three people taken to an area hospital. He was said to be in serious condition and was being analyzed by LAPD drug recognition experts to determine if he was under the influence at the time of the crash.The circumstances surrounding the collision remain under investigation, but LAPD Major Collision Investigation Team and Valley Traffic Division detectives said that the driver was attempting to avoid another car that was driving "legally and safely" before the crash. Police said they would continue looking for security camera footage from the Metro bus station and businesses in the surrounding area as their probe continued."It'll be a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here," LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said. "Our hearts go out to the families of the victims that were struck here tonight."Aerial footage showed the white SUV stopped on the sidewalk underneath a canopy, where the food stand was set up. Witnesses told CBS LA the three deceased victims were street vendors in the area, one of whom worked there for more than 15 years.This is a developing story. Check back for details.

national.title: Matthew Farwell convicted of killing Sandra Birchmore, unborn child
national.summary: A jury has found former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell guilty of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child.
national.body: A jury has found former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell guilty of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child. The verdict was read in federal court in South Boston Tuesday afternoon.Farwell was charged with killing a witness or victim and causing the death of an unborn child. He pleaded not guilty. The jury had previously said in a note on Monday that it was "in a deadlock."There were gasps from Birchmore's family as the verdict was read aloud in court.Farwell faces a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole. Sentencing is scheduled for Feb. 3, 2027. The Department of Justice could have pursued the death penalty against Farwell, but decided last year it would not. Jurors heard from 50 witnesses over four weeks of testimony. To convict Farwell on the charge of killing a witness or victim, jurors had to find find that he not only killed Birchmore, but that he did so to prevent her from reporting his crimes to federal authorities. "Today, justice was served for Ms. Sandra Birchmore and her unborn son, both of whom died at the hands of Matthew Farwell. national.title: Kennedys sue to block Trump's arch, arguing it would cast shadow on JFK's grave
national.summary: Nine members of the political dynasty say the 250ft structure would cast a shadow on gravesites.
national.body:
The family of former US President John F Kennedy has sued to block construction of a triumphal arch that President Donald Trump plans to build in the nation's capital.

Nine members of the political dynasty argue the 250ft (76m) structure would block the view of Kennedy's grave, as well as the graves of thousands of veterans buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.

Last week, a US judge temporarily halted the project on the heels of a vote allowing construction to proceed.

The White House said it was "unfortunate" to see that some members of the Kennedy family had joined litigation against an arch "intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery".

"The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis R Ingle said in a statement to the BBC.

"We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added.

Last week the project won approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.

But US District Judge Tanya Chutkan then ruled there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch as litigation plays out.

national.title: Kennedys sue to block Trump's arch, arguing it would cast shadow on JFK's grave
national.summary: Nine members of the political dynasty say the 250ft structure would cast a shadow on gravesites.
national.body:
The family of former US President John F Kennedy has sued to block construction of a triumphal arch that President Donald Trump plans to build in the nation's capital.

Nine members of the political dynasty argue the 250ft (76m) structure would block the view of Kennedy's grave, as well as the graves of thousands of veterans buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.

Last week, a US judge temporarily halted the project on the heels of a vote allowing construction to proceed.

The White House said it was "unfortunate" to see that some members of the Kennedy family had joined litigation against an arch "intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery".

"The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis R Ingle said in a statement to the BBC.

"We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added.

Last week the project won approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.

But US District Judge Tanya Chutkan then ruled there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch as litigation plays out.

He also said 2,732 absentee mail ballots were still out, and the deadline for election officials to receive them would be Tuesday, Nov. 10. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge in a state President Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races in the midterms, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. national.title: In Mississippi, voters await cliffhanger Senate result with hope and frustration
national.summary: Democratic voters tell the BBC their candidate is on the brink of history, while Republicans vent disappointment.
national.body:
Mississippi's nailbiting wait to find out who won the southern state's Senate race is nearly over a week after the US midterm elections, in a contest that could deliver their first Democratic senator in nearly four decades.

Scott Colom, the Democrat, holds a lead of about 2,500 ballots - less than 1% - over his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to the latest tally.

If he wins, Colom would become the Magnolia State's first black senator in over 140 years.

He would also pad the Democratic Senate majority-elect to 55 seats, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.

The Democrat's razor-thin advantage has defied political gravity in a conservative fortress that President Donald Trump won in 2024 by over 22 points.

State law holds that the deadline to certify results is this Friday, but thousands of postal and affidavit ballots remain uncounted.

Affidavit ballots are ones that were not immediately accepted because of a discrepancy such as lacking proper ID on election day.

In such cases, voters are asked to fill out a provisional ballot and return to resolve the issue. The deadline for both affidavit and mail-in ballots is on Tuesday.

national.body: Several members of the Kennedy family have joined the legal battle to prevent President Trump from building a large triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery. In court filings Tuesday, nine members of the famous family — including several children and grandchildren of Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy and Sen. Ted Kennedy — argued the 250-foot-tall arch would block the sightlines of the Kennedy family's gravesites and the "Eternal Flame" commemorating President John F. Kennedy. The family members wrote that the project will "permanently cast a shadow over the graves of servicemen and women who made the ultimate sacrifice for this country, including the Kennedy Gravesites."The family members are seeking to intervene as plaintiffs in a lawsuit opposing the arch from the city of Washington, D.C., and the Commonwealth of Virginia. national.title: Headquarters of Haitian gang destroyed, El Salvador's president says
national.summary: The infamous 400 Mawozo gang was targeted by the El Salvador military which has deployed thousands of troops to combat Haiti's gang violence crisis.
national.body:
The headquarters of one of Haiti's largest crime gangs has been destroyed by El Salvador's military, the Salvadoran president has said.

The infamous 400 Mawozo gang, which is known for kidnappings and intimidation tactics, was targeted in a ground and air attack at a complex on the outskirts of Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince.

It is El Salvador's first military action on a Haitian target since it deployed more than 2,000 soldiers there last month, as part of a mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran technicians.

Haiti has been plagued by gang violence for years, with heavily armed groups controlling large parts of the capital, and beyond.

El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele announced the news on X , external , boasting that most of the gang members fled without trying to fight.

"We destroyed the house of [gang leader] Lanmò San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters," he wrote on Tuesday.

The post was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex, reportedly in the suburb of Croix-des-Bouquets, the gang's stronghold.

As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes.

national.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
national.summary: The 82-year-old was placed under house detention in Florida last week after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.
national.body:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.

Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.

US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.

Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.

Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".

He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.

"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.

national.title: House blocks Massie's effort to impeach Hegseth
national.summary: GOP Rep. Thomas Massie said Monday he would not bring up another resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
national.body: Washington — The House on Tuesday blocked an effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, largely over the war with Iran. The House voted 211 to 204 to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively killing it. Massie was the lone Republican to vote with all Democrats against it. Though Republicans have been frustrated with Hegseth's handling of the war that has stretched into its ninth month, many did not think his conduct rose to the level of impeachment. "I wasn't surprised, but I was disappointed," Massie said after the vote. "My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do. They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically." Massie, a Kentucky Republican, said Monday he would not bring up another resolution to impeach Hegseth. He is retiring in early January after losing his primary earlier this year. Democrats could still force the issue, especially when they retake control of both chambers in January. "This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat, said following the vote. Massie said Tuesday he planned to force a vote on a war powers resolution. "We're going to see all these Republicans who said, 'Oh, we lost this election because of the war,' will they still vote for it?" Massie said. The impeachment resolution accused Hegseth of abusing his office by launching the Iran war without congressional approval, ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties, directing extrajudicial killings for the Pentagon's boat strikes in the Caribbean, directing the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, among other allegations. In a news conference Tuesday morning, Hegseth denounced the impeachment effort, calling it a "farce" and "political spectacle." "None of these are high crimes or misdemeanors," Hegseth argued. "They're partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military."President Trump mocked the impeachment effort, saying it "miserably FAILED!"Seven Republicans and 11 Democrats missed the vote.Only two Cabinet secretaries in U.S. history have been impeached. national.title: Judge allows Trump's $10bn defamation case against BBC to proceed
national.summary: But the court dismisses the other part of Trump's lawsuit that alleged the BBC had violated a Florida law.
national.body:
A federal judge in Florida has allowed US President Donald Trump's defamation case against the BBC to go ahead after the broadcaster sought to dismiss it.

But Judge Jeffrey Kuntz dismissed a second claim in the $10bn (£7.5bn) lawsuit under the state's unfair trade practices law.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a Truth Social post on Tuesday. A BBC spokesperson said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."

The BBC spokesperson added: "We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process."

Judge Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not make a ruling on the merits of the case.

"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," he wrote in Tuesday's order.

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

local.title: Rochester launches effort to help homeowners go solar
local.summary: The initiative will bring homeowners together to leverage their collective purchasing power and negotiate competitive pricing from qualified local installers, according to a city news release.
local.body:
A new effort by the city of Rochester aims to help residents afford solar energy and save on electricity costs.

The city is partnering with the global provider Switch Together, which will act as a group buyer for residential solar installations. The initiative will bring homeowners together to leverage their collective purchasing power and negotiate competitive pricing from qualified local installers, according to a city news release. There's a Dec. 16 deadline to register and accept an offer.

Through the program, homeowners will be able to review a personalized solar installation offer and decide whether to move forward. Homeowners can register on Switch Together's website, where they can also find out more information about the program and their property's suitability for solar.

The city and its partner are also holding a virtual Solar 101 information session for residents from 6 to 7 p.m. on Nov. 19. Registration is required and can be completed on Switch Together's site.

The city receives no compensation through the program but also incurs no cost, according to the release.

local.summary: State lawmakers are considering new restrictions on automated license plate reader (ALPR) technology amid concerns about how the information is collected, stored and shared.
local.body: State lawmakers are considering new restrictions on automated license plate reader (ALPR) technology amid concerns about how the information is collected, stored and shared.The issue was the focus of an Assembly hearing that brought together law enforcement officials, civil liberties advocates and other experts. The debate grew tense at times, with lawmakers challenging claims that the technology is not a threat to constitutional privacy rights.The cameras, often associated with the Flock brand, photograph passing vehicles and capture license plate information, along with the time and location of each scan. The information can then be stored and searched by law enforcement.Assemblymember Nily Rozic, who chairs the Assembly's Consumer Affairs and Protection Committee, said New York lacks consistent statewide rules governing the technology."In New York, we currently lack universal minimum standards governing the collection, retention, and use sharing of information through these systems," Rozic said. local.title: 'Concerning': Buffalo councilmember presses for answers after police staffing problems revealed
local.summary: A 7 News investigation revealed Buffalo police overtime used to meet minimum staffing jumped 65% last fiscal year. Now a local lawmaker is demanding answers on the recruiting slump.
local.body: The city of Buffalo does not always have enough police officers to meet minimum staffing requirements, relying more and more on overtime to fill shifts. That's the result of a months-long investigation I revealed on Monday. Now, a local lawmaker has questions.Buffalo Common Councilmember David Rivera is chair of the council's Police Oversight Committee. He's reacting to the fact that police overtime used to cover minimum staffing requirements skyrocketed in 2025 to 2026 compared to the previous fiscal year. It was up 65%."It's alarming, it's concerning. You're dealing with public safety," Rivera said. "It's unfortunate that we haven't had a recruit class in the recent past."The last police exam was administered by the city in 2023. Speaking to me Monday, Police Commissioner Erika Shields put the problem down to the subsequent three-year pause, explaining that the Buffalo Police Department now aims to recruit through the next available state police exam in April 2027. WATCH: Buffalo councilmember presses for answers after police staffing revelationsRivera has asked the city's HR department to explain the reasons for the pause.One person who might know is Rivera's fellow councilmember, Christopher Scanlon. He was acting mayor from October 2024 through December 2025 at the time of that pause. He was unavailable to speak to me Tuesday.In the meantime, what about the council's role in all this? I asked Rivera whether this is something the council could have kept a closer eye on in the past."Well, we have a list, we have a current list that hasn't expired, that's still there until 2027," he said, referring to a list of people who have already passed the city's civil service police exam - the first step in becoming a police officer. "The question I have is why haven't we hired from that list?"I asked the mayor's office if that list is exhausted but have not yet heard anything back on that subject. An HR representative is expected to discuss the matter at the council meeting next Tuesday. local.body: Britini D'Angelo, a special education teacher in Niagara Falls, was named by Kleenex as the National Hero of the Classroom. The award comes with cash prizes for both her and Kalfas Elementary.For the past three years, Miss D'Angelo has brought smiles to students’ faces inside her Henry J. Kalfas Elementary School classroom.“I love my job more than I can express in words. This is what I am meant to do for the rest of my life,” D'Angelo said. Long before she ever decided on her professional career, her road to teaching started before her second birthday.“When I was 22 months old, I was diagnosed with autism. I was nonverbal, no eye contact, repetitive stims and no social cues,” D'Angelo said. “I had a one-to-one aide until the end of first grade, so I had a village fighting for my IEP every single day.”That village both taught her to be the person she is today and inspired her to pour into others in similar situations to what she had experienced growing up.“I want the absolute best for them every single day, and as their advocate, we are going to make sure that happens,” D'Angelo said.“She understands the kids a lot,” Najah Peterson, one of D'Angelo’s assistant teachers, said. “She always puts kids first, school first, and she’s so sweet. She’s willing to help everybody.”WATCH: ‘I love my job’: Niagara Falls teacher named National Hero of the Classroom by KleenexD’Angelo’s story has caught the attention of hundreds of thousands of followers online, 215,000 on Instagram and 679,000 on TikTok. local.body: Ten years ago, thick black smoke poured into the sky over Lackawanna when a massive fire ripped through the Steelworks Industrial Park off Route 5 — the site of the former Bethlehem Steel facility. The fire started November 9th, with hundreds of firefighters assisting from nearby communities."I came outside and you could see all the smoke," Michael Murray said.Murray has lived just around the corner on Pine Street for 48 years. local.title: Gov. Hochul keeps the door open to redrawing New York’s congressional map
local.summary: The Democratic governor remains open to a constitutional amendment that would make it easier for her party to redraw the lines.
local.body:
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she remains open to a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for Democrats to redraw New York’s congressional districts as soon as 2028.

The Democratic governor told reporters Tuesday that major Democratic wins across the country in last week’s elections wouldn’t necessarily derail her party’s push to change the state constitution to allow for mid-decade redistricting in the Empire State.

But Hochul also didn’t commit to moving ahead with the plan, which was first put into motion last year as Republicans in Texas, North Carolina and other states began redrawing congressional districts to benefit their party.

The Republican efforts — backed by President Donald Trump — either backfired or didn’t matter, with Democrats easily picking up enough seats across the country to take control of the U.S. House of Representatives.

“Those newly drawn lines [in other states] are still there,” Hochul said at her Manhattan office. “And while it didn’t have an effect on this year’s election, there’s always another election every two years.”

The governor continued: “You can't assume that there's going to be the same outcomes every two years, and so I want to look at it long-term.”

In New York, the state constitution requires a bipartisan panel to redraw congressional lines after each once-a-decade Census, with lawmakers getting final approval. But it doesn’t provide a mechanism to change the districts during the intervening years.

In March, the U.S. Supreme Court halted a lower court’s order that would’ve required redrawing New York’s 11th congressional district , a Republican stronghold that includes all of Staten Island and parts of Brooklyn. The order was spurred by a Democrat-led lawsuit that argued the current district disenfranchised Black and Hispanic voters. Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, a Republican who has held the district since 2021, was re-elected last Tuesday.

local.body: Tina Abrams, a longtime voice in the Seneca Nation, was officially sworn into office alongside her new executive branch. Now in office, Abrams says protecting sovereignty is a top priority.Before becoming president, Abrams served in leadership roles for decades.
